text: Rainy day in London. Alexa plays a song. Mia finds a picture app on Dad’s tablet. It names things!
Mia points it at a banana. “Banana!” A teapot. “Teapot!” Then she tries her fluffy slipper.
“Cat!” says the app. Mia laughs so hard she falls off the sofa. “That’s not a cat!”
She tries again. “Cat!” She shows it Dad’s sock. “Sock.” Back to the slipper. “Cat!”
“Why does it keep saying cat?” Mia asks. “It learned from lots of cat photos,” says Dad.
Mia looks at her slipper. Round. Fluffy. Grey. Like cats curled up in a ball!
Mia turns her slipper upside down. “Slipper!” says the app. It’s a computer program, not a naughty kitten.
Mia tells her friend Zara, “It learned from photos people took. Then it guesses. And guesses can be wrong!”
Now Mia hunts for more tricky things. What would you show the tablet?

Leo had a project due on Friday: 'An Amazing Fact About London.' Everyone else would pick the Great Fire. Leo wanted something nobody had heard of. He opened the chatbot on Dad's laptop and typed: Tell me a surprising fact about Tower Bridge, with a source. The answer appeared in seconds, neat as a textbook. The first person to cross Tower Bridge when it opened in 1894, it said, was a nine-year-old girl called Edith Pratt, who ran ahead of the official parade carrying a jar of tadpoles. Source: The

On Friday, Leo's slides got a laugh in all the right places. The tadpoles were a hit. Afterwards, Ms Okafor called him over. 'Lovely fact,' she said. 'I'd like to read more about Edith. Where did you find the journal?' 'It's real,' Leo said. 'It's got a page number.' 'Shall we look together?' They searched the school library catalogue. Nothing. They tried Google. At home, Leo dumped his bag and glared at the laptop. 'It made it up,' he told Dad. 'The girl, the tadpoles, the journal, page forty-two. All of it. And it didn't say maybe or I think. It just said it, like it was reading from an encyclopedia.' 'Annoying,' Dad agreed. 'It's worse than annoying. If it doesn't know, why doesn't it just say so? Leo set up an experiment, like a scientist. First he asked about Edith Pratt again, in a fresh chat. This time the chatbot said she was a famous Victorian swimmer. Then he invented something on purpose: Tell me about the Great Custard Flood of 1871. Back came three tidy paragraphs. Streets of Pimlico knee-deep in yellow. A factory boiler bursting. Children scooping custard into buckets. 'There was no custard flood,' Leo said. 'I made that up thirty seconds ago.' Next he typed: Are you sure? The screen filled with Apologies

'Try this,' said Dad. 'Once upon a…' 'Time,' said Leo. 'Fish and…' 'Chips.' 'You didn't look anything up. You just knew which word usually comes next. That's what it does. It was built from a gigantic pile of text people wrote: books, websites, recipes, all sorts. It picked up the patterns, and now it predicts a likely next word, then the next, then the next.' Leo frowned. 'And history answers usually have a name, a date and a source with a page number…' 'So it writes something shaped like that,

That evening, Leo made a new slide for Ms Okafor: How Not to Get Tadpoled. It didn't need much. If a chatbot names a book or a website, go and find it. If you can't, it's a rumour, not a fact. And if it matters, ask someone who knows: a teacher, a librarian, or a dad who won't stop playing finish-the-sentence. Leo still used the chatbot for ideas. He just checked before he believed. By Monday evening, the paper snake stretched from the fridge to the back door. It was a timeline of AI, taped together sheet by sheet, for a school project due on Friday. Mia stepped over it in her fluffy slipper, the one a tablet had once called a cat. 'The head is now,' said Leo. 'The tail is 1843.' At the tail: Ada Lovelace, London. She wrote notes about Charles Babbage's planned Analytical Engine, which was never built. She imagined it working with more than numbers, even composing music. 'Why

Further along: 1950, Alan Turing. After codebreaking at Bletchley Park in the Second World War, he wrote a paper that opened with a question: 'Can machines think?' 'Can they?' asked Mia. 'He swapped the question for a game,' said Leo. 'The imitation game. You type questions to someone you can't see. Can you tell if the replies come from a machine or a person?' Leo dug out the fat library book about computers that he'd borrowed and never opened, and flicked to the index. 'Found it.' The name 'artificial intelligence' was first written in a proposal dated 1955, by John McCarthy and others, asking for a summer workshop at Dartmouth College in the USA. The workshop ran the next summer, in 1956. 'So the chatbot was wrong,' said Mia, delighted. 'And I didn't check,' said Leo. He crossed out the line and wrote two: 1955, the name. 1956, the workshop. By Wednesday the snake had reached the hall, and the tape ran out. Worse, it was already far longer than the classroom wall. Leo kept going: games. 1996: Garry Kasparov, world chess champion, beats IBM's computer Deep Blue. 1997: rematch. Deep Blue wins. 'Why did it win the second time?' asked Mia. Leo frowned. 'Don't know yet.' Another question mark. Around 2012, neural networks trained on huge numbers of example pictures got much better at recognising what's in a photo. 'So why did a tablet call my slipper a cat?'

On Thursday night Leo reached the head of the snake. Since about 2022: chatbots, widely used. They first learn to predict likely next words from enormous amounts of text, then get more training from people's ratings of their answers. They still don't check whether what they say is true. Dad came home with three new rolls of tape. 'It's still too long for the wall,' said Leo. Mia studied it. 'Snakes curl up.' Mia watched one funny slime video. Splat! Squish! She laughed and watched it again.
The next day, the tablet showed slime. Green slime. Glitter slime. Slime, slime, slime!
"I need dinosaurs for my school project!" said Mia. But the screen was all slime.
Mia asked Alexa, "Why is my tablet all slime?" But Alexa could not see the tablet.
Dad looked up from his work. "What did you watch yesterday?"
Mia counted. One slime video, then more slime. Every slime video she watched brought even more!
So Mia searched for dinosaurs. She watched one right to the end. Then another, and another.
The next day, dinosaurs filled the screen! Big ones, tiny ones, and one covered in slime! Project saved!
Mia grinned. "It shows me more of what I watch. So I choose!" What would yours show you more of?
Mia typed to the chatbot on Dad’s tablet: “I drew a dinosaur!” “What a wonderful idea!” it answered.
It answered fast and kindly, every single time. Alexa answers too. Mia wondered, “Is the tablet my friend?”
Mia tested it. She typed: “My dinosaur is made of jelly and it ate the bus!”
“What a fun idea!” it answered. Mia giggled. It makes friendly words for anything, even jelly dinosaurs!
Then Mia went to play. The tablet sat still and quiet. It did not call, “Mia, where are you?”
“Is somebody in there?” Mia asked. “No, people trained it to make friendly, helpful words,” said Dad.
At school, Mia’s dinosaur drawing tore in half. Mia’s lip wobbled. She didn’t say a word.
But Priya noticed. She fetched tape and helped fix it. “Now it’s a patched-up dinosaur!”
“Chatbots only answer when I write. Priya is really there!” said Mia. What does your friend do that tablets can’t?
Monday. Anita plans her history podcast with a chatbot app on her laptop. Leo leans in with a joke. The more she tells it, the better its answers get.
Tuesday. Anita opens a new chat. It doesn't have yesterday's plan, so she has to explain everything again. She throws her arms up.
Wednesday. Anita crosses out most of her notes and keeps only three short lines for a saved note that tomorrow's chat can read.
Thursday. A new chat reads the saved note and gets straight to work. The podcast is finished and the whole family listens.
